text: You've spent five chapters building zero trust controls. This chapter asks a different question: how do you know how far along you actually are, in a way someone outside your team can trust? CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model answers exactly that — it's become the de facto common language for zero trust progress, in government and well beyond it, because it gives every organization the same categories and the same stages to describe progress in.

The model scores maturity separately across five pillars, not as one blended score, and that's deliberate. Identity covers how strongly users and non-human identities are verified. Devices covers inventory and compliance. Networks covers segmentation and encryption versus static zones. Applications and Workloads covers how access to an app is authorized and tested. Data covers inventory, classification, and whether access depends on sensitivity. Averaging these together would hide exactly the gap an attacker would actually exploit.

Layered across all five are three cross-cutting capabilities. Visibility and Analytics asks whether you can see and correlate signals across pillars instead of each one being a blind spot to the others. Automation and Orchestration asks whether risk signals trigger automated responses. Governance asks whether policy and accountability structures make controls durable rather than dependent on one engineer's memory. A pillar can look technically advanced and still fail here — great segmentation with no governance process for who approves new rules isn't maturity, it's fragility.

Every pillar, and every cross-cutting capability, gets scored against the same four stages. Traditional means manual configuration and static, broad policy. Initial means automation is starting, still mostly siloed. Advanced means centrally controlled, automated policy with routine coordination across pillars. Optimal means fully automated, just-in-time access, continuously validated against real-time risk — the assume-breach, verify-explicitly posture actually running, not just written down.

Take Identity as a concrete example. Traditional is password-only login with manual identity risk reviews. Initial adds multi-factor authentication and early centralization. Advanced moves to phishing-resistant MFA with automated risk scoring feeding access decisions. Optimal means continuous validation and just-enough access, with real-time risk analytics evaluating every single request. Same four stages — applied pillar by pillar, which is exactly why one organization can be Advanced on Identity and still Traditional on Data.

That's the map: five pillars, three cross-cutting capabilities, four stages, scored independently rather than blended into one reassuring number. Next lesson, you'll put it to work for real — walking your own environment pillar by pillar against these stage definitions, and learning why self-scoring honestly is harder, and more valuable, than it sounds.
